problem: Prior high-level-instruction navigation agents (e.g. VLN-DUET) only use observed history and do not exploit commonsense knowledge of room layouts or imagine the destination, so they generalize poorly to unseen environments.
motivation: With concise instructions that only describe a remote object, humans imagine what the destination looks like and use layout priors (a bathroom is near a bedroom) to explore efficiently. The paper injects this visual commonsense into a topological-map agent using a pre-trained text-to-image model.
key_idea: Use GLIDE-generated images as visual commonsense: a room-type codebook supervises auxiliary layout prediction on topological nodes (Layout Learner), and imagined destination images are cross-attended with node features to guide action choice (Goal Dreamer).
insight: Layout prediction as an auxiliary task and destination imagination each improve the VLN-DUET baseline (SR 52.34 -> 56.04 with Layout Learner; both together reach 57.00 on val-unseen). Visual codebook beats a plain room-classification head (SR 53.73) and a CLIP text codebook (SR 51.38), so image descriptors are better soft room concepts than labels or text. Goal Dreamer raises SPL/RGSPL while slightly lowering RGS, suggesting more efficient exploration rather than better grounding.
method: Topological graph base (VLN-DUET): builds an on-the-fly topological map with visited, current and unexplored nodes, using global and local cross-graph-language encoders with dynamic fusion; adds an extra graph-aware self-attention over nodes before language cross-attention.

Room type codebook: GLIDE is prompted with 'A [room type] with [obj1]... and [objn]' (objects co-occurring with frequency >0.8 in REVERIE training instructions) for the 30 Matterport room types. 100 images per type are generated, S representative ones are selected by K-Means in CLIP space, and their CLIP features form E_room.

Layout Learner: node embeddings from the global branch are scored against the codebook features (summed dot products over S images), and cross-entropy against GT room labels supervises the scores. It is an auxiliary task used only in training, not at inference.

Goal Dreamer: five GLIDE images are generated from the instruction and encoded with CLIP. Global node embeddings cross-attend to these features, and an FFN predicts a next-node distribution supervised by the GT next action.

Decision Maker: local-global dynamic fusion is combined with the dreamer branch via a node-specific learned weight lambda (FFN on concatenated features), giving the DSAP action distribution. Object grounding is a classification FFN over candidate objects.

Training: warmup of 100k iterations (batch 32) with MLM, MRC, OG, LP and DSAP, then DAgger imitation for 50k iterations (batch 8). Inference is greedy with Dijkstra for backtracking; the highest-scoring object is chosen at stop.

setting.backbone: VLN-DUET-style topological transformer with CLIP features (trained), plus frozen GLIDE and CLIP for codebook and imagination generation
setting.training_data: REVERIE / SOON training splits; GLIDE-generated images (100 per room type for 30 types, 5 destination images per instruction); pre-training tasks MLM, MRC, OG, LP, DSAP; DAgger fine-tuning
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views) with provided object bounding boxes (SOON uses detected boxes from a Bottom-Up detector)
setting.action_space: discrete navigation-graph nodes (topological map, including backtracking) plus stop
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT room labels only for training supervision; object boxes provided by the REVERIE benchmark)

results: On the REVERIE test-unseen split LAD reaches SR 56.53 and RGS 35.31, beating VLN-DUET (52.51 / 31.88) by 4.02 SR and 3.43 RGS. On val-unseen it reaches SR 57.00 vs 46.98. On SOON test-unseen SR is 39.59 vs 33.44 for VLN-DUET. On REVERIE val-seen it is below VLN-DUET (SR 69.22 vs 71.75).
limitations: Imagination is static, conditioned only on the instruction and not updated with observations
Only five destination images and a limited set of codebook images are used, because of generation time and storage; overfitting is observed late in training
Room type recognition accuracy remains unsatisfactory because Matterport room labels are ambiguous and rooms often lack clear boundaries
